title: Who is the beloved?
hookLine: in Sufi poetry the beloved is often God, and wine and tavern are old symbols (Divan-e Shams)

cards: A respected Muslim scholar, a teacher of Islamic law, writes line after line about wine. A tavern at midnight. A cupbearer pouring again.
A beloved with a face like the moon, and a lover who has lost his reputation, his turban and his mind. Read cold, it sounds like a very different kind of life.
Readers raised on Persian poetry would have heard something else at once. So who is the beloved?

teach.b: Persian poetry, long before and long after Rumi, has a shared set of pictures, almost a code. The beloved, the one the poem longs for. Wine.
The tavern. The cupbearer, called the saqi. The nightingale and the rose.
In Sufi poetry, the Islamic mystical tradition Rumi belongs to, these pictures usually point beyond themselves.
The beloved is very often God.
Wine is the overwhelming experience of divine love, the kind that makes a person forget himself. The tavern is where a respectable ego gets ruined, and the ruin is the point.
Islam forbids drinking wine, and Rumi, a scholar of the law, knew that. Part of the image's power is its shock: a Sufi reader hears an intoxication no cup can hold. So is it all code?
Not quite, and here honesty matters. Rumi's beloved is sometimes plainly Shams, a real man he loved and lost. Sometimes it's God.

teach.h: SHAMS, GOD, OR BOTH AT ONCE.
teach.b: Often it's both at once, the human friend as the window through which the divine showed up.

Scholars and Sufis read this layering in different ways, and nobody can pin down every poem. Some modern readers take the poems as simply human love songs. In the Sufi tradition, the spiritual meaning comes first.
The poems hold up under both. Two ways to read: not choosing one to beat the other, but letting a poem be a love letter and a prayer at the same time, and noticing which one you heard first.

how: In Sufi circles, Rumi's love poems are recited and sung as devotional poetry about God, and readers also hear in them his love for his friend Shams.

games.q: you read a Rumi ghazal full of wine and a moon-faced beloved. how do you read it?
o: as a human love song, only.
as both: a love letter and a prayer.
as a secret code with one answer.
games.why: the Sufi tradition hears the beloved as God and the wine as divine love, and Rumi's beloved is sometimes also Shams. a poem can hold both readings at once.

practice: Pick any love song or poem you know, even a pop chorus, and first hear it as it seems: one person longing for another. Then hear the same words as longing for something larger: the source, the whole, God if that's your word.
Don't decide which is right; just notice what shifts.

wordCard.voice: Shams. Rumi's beloved is sometimes plainly this real man he loved and lost, sometimes God, often both at once. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: the beloved, the one who is loved.
